newsitem.title: TURKEY: Third time lucky for Turkey's Mesut Yilmaz?.
newsitem.headline: Third time lucky for Turkey's Mesut Yilmaz?.

text.p: Turkey's main opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz, charged by President Suleyman Demirel on Friday to form a new government, is a political tortoise among hares.

Outgoing Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, pushed out of office by secularist pressure, enthuses in flowing rhetoric about an Islamic "Just Order". Yilmaz's bitter rival Tansu Ciller exhorts her country "Forward into Europe".
But Yilmaz, slow-spoken and earnest, has never seemed to stir the blood in a political career which has brought him two ill-fated spells as prime minister.
He has kept his conservative, pro-market Motherland Party on an even keel in the rough-and-tumble world of Turkish politics, but analysts describe his record in opposition as lacklustre.

Motherland is the second biggest party in parliament with 129 deputies in the 550-seat assembly, but Yilmaz faces a tough challenge to win majority support for any coalition. He was confident of his ability to rise to the challenge.
"There is an extremely high possibility that a government formed under me can win a vote of confidence," he told the NTV television news channel on Thursday.
Now 50, still young for a Turkish leader, Yilmaz is poised to make his third bid to establish himself as a long-term prime minister.

He headed the government for three months in 1991 until a general election defeat by the True Path Party, then led by Demirel, who became president in May 1993. Demirel left his post to Ciller, a U.S.-educated economist.
A fierce animosity between Yilmaz and Ciller brought about the downfall of a 1996 coalition between the pair after just three months, ending Yilmaz's second tenure.
That coalition's collapse helped Islamists to lead the government for the first time in Turkey's modern history.
The two conservative parties are close on policy but their leaders are poles apart. Ciller is a dramatic, instinctive, political survivor and Yilmaz measured, thoughful and, some say, a tad boring.
Their rivalry has defined Yilmaz's recent career. He has spent many years -- largely unsuccessfully -- attempting to frustrate Ciller and pin corruption charges on her.

Now he says he is prepared to put that behind him and "knock on the door" of Ciller's True Path to discuss an alliance. He will need support from some True Path deputies to establish a government without the Islamists.

Yilmaz took control of Motherland in April 1993, after the sudden death of its founder and later Turkish president Turgut Ozal. He has since distanced the party from the principles laid down by Ozal and his powerful family.
Born into a wealthy family in the Black Sea town of Rize, Yilmaz entered parliament in 1983 after three years of army rule that cracked down on extremist political violence.
Previously he held managerial positions in various companies in the chemicals, textiles and transport sectors.
Yilmaz, who helped found Motherland, was state minister and then tourism and culture minister in the 1983 civilian government founded by then prime minister Ozal.
He later served as foreign minister for three years until he resigned in a policy dispute with then premier Yildirim Akbulut.
Yilmaz is a political science graduate from Ankara University. He is married, has two children and speaks English and German.
